items.question: Where are you from?
items.answer:
This is by far the most common question, asked to travellers, but people don't realize how difficult it is to answer. It all depends on the *scale*. 

In terms of space, the answer could range from the exact coordinates of the maternity ward where I was born, to the entire universe as my place of origin.
In terms of time, it depends on whether you consider my existence to begin when I was forced out of my mother's womb, or if you go farther into the past to the beginning of the universe, or even if you consider I am reborn a new person every morning.

Most people assume implicitly that the scale is "What country were you brought out of your mother's womb at", in which case the answer is **Portugal**. More specifically, the city of Coimbra.

items.question: What route will you take to Japan? How will you cross the ocean?
items.answer:
I plan to take as many existing pilgrimage routes as possible because it is probably the easiest way. I started with Camino de Santiago. Then I'll make my way to Italy using the Via Francigena, later I'll use the roads to Jerusalem and then I'll have to decide whether to cross through Iran or go around over the Caspian sea, depending on the political developments by the time I get there. 

Either way, the route will be very close to the ancient Silk Road.

For more information, check the Map page (currently under construction).

items.question: How many kilometers/days to Japan?
items.answer:
Nobody really knows the answer because the path will reveal itself as one goes along. 
If you check it on Google Maps, the distance is about **15.000 km**. If we include some estimated rest periods, the total time is about **3 to 3,5 years.**

items.question: Why are you doing this trip?
Why Japan / What's in Japan?
items.answer:
In truth, this has nothing to do with Japan. I just chose the longest distance I could possibly imagine walking at the time. One of my inspirations was the Pokémon games, where the character walks across an entire region of their own world, and some of the games even involve multiple regions. Usually, the character starts out at a remote corner of the region, which makes the adventure more linear.
Because I'm originally from Portugal, which is at the very western tip of Europe, my first thought was to do a Pokémon journey across my Europe. Then I figured, if I'm seriously going to do this, why not take it all the way to the eastern tip of Asia? If I could conquer that massive stretch, the entire world would be my home. 

Eventually I started getting fond of Japanese culture and learned its language. When I did the Camino for the first time, I met with Kasa, the hat. Apparently the hat had come from Japan with another pilgrim, also on foot. That was a major inspiration for me, but it wasn't until a few months later, when I was looking at ancient Japanese pilgrim gear for inspiration, that I learned that the hat is actually a part of the pilgrim attire for the Shikoku pilgrimage. 
That's when I decided I *had* to take on the persona of Henro and bring Kasa back to its original home.

items.question: What about money? How do you fund your trip?
items.answer:
That's exactly the point of this trip. I'm not planning to fund it with external sources, such as saving enough money from a job before departing, or using this website, or support from my family, or being a digital nomad - on the contrary, I want to be an *"analogical nomal"*. I want to test my thesis that, just like the ancient prehistorical nomads, we *can* make the whole world our home, or at least a larger portion of it that we're accostumed to. 

In other words, I believe that the journey can **fund itself**. So, I will consider it my "full time job" to be a pilgrim to Japan. I might even say 'Henro' is some strange kind of company, and I am it's employee. 

Another inspiration I have is Jesus Christ. If you know anything about the Bible, you probably know that he used to travel around the region of Galilee with his apostles, and they used money like everyone else (even though Jesus could apparently conjure food). Their "company" was funded much like a modern church is: Jesus was a preacher, so he received alms from the people who heard him preach, whatever they were willing and able to give. He did not charge, but he got paid because people valued his religious services and wanted to support him. I see my quest as some form of religious/spiritual and educational service, even though it's a little bit different from either. 

But if I'm in a pinch and need to make money, I can definitely see myself looking for work wherever I am at the moment, especially during the winters. The only condition is that I find that work *within* the pilgrimage, and not through external sources.

items.question: How many languages do you speak?
What do your parents/partner think about this?
items.answer:
It took me a long time to tell my parents about this plan. It wasn't until I finished the Camino de Santiago up to France that I was able to come back to Portugal and actually talk to them. Until that moment, I was never confident enough to receive their presumable concerns. But when I shared it with them, I did it with confidence and addressed all the most obvious concerns. Thus, I sensed they were able to have some peace of mind that I wasn't completely out of my mind, but actually had an idea of what I was doing.

As for my partner, her only biggest concern is whether we will be able to keep a connected relationship while I'm on the road, but we're both quite certain of our love and very excited about the project itself.

items.question: You walk with these sandals?! 🩴
items.answer:
These are obviously not your regular flip-flops. They are huarache-style sandals, made for the outdoors, by the brand Earth Runners. They are said to last a long time, though I doubt they will last the entire pilgrimage, even if I do have a pair of boots on the side.

I prefer the sandals over the boots because I don't need to worry about wetting my socks every time I want to swim in a river along the way, and it's much quicker to get in and out of them than the boots. The most important thing, I have found, is to change your footwear every few days, so that the feet don't get beaten in the same place over and over. I switch between **3 "gears"**: Boots, sandals and barefoot, depending on the terrain and the pain my feet are in.
